headline: Many Americans plan homemade Halloween costumes

sources.title: The Vogue Business TikTok Trend Tracker (Vogue Business)
Survey Says: Halloween Shoppers Choose Creativity Over Costumes Off the Rack (Lynnwood Times)
NRF Halloween Survey Shows Consumer Spending Expected to Reach $13.5 Billion (National Retail Federation)

chunks.text: Halloween falls on Saturday, October 31, and many Americans are already deciding what to {{dress up as}}. This year, many shoppers are skipping the [[costume aisle]]. Instead, they {{put together}} their own looks from [[thrift-store clothing]] and [[household objects]]. Some {{make do with}} whatever they already have at home. For many of them, the goal is a [[one-of-a-kind]] look that does not cost much.

verbs.correct: To wear a costume of a character
verbs.wrong: To sell old clothes to a store
verbs.why: My son wants to dress up as a pirate this year. She dressed up as a cat for the office party. Many Americans are already deciding what to dress up as for Halloween on October 31.

verbs.correct: To make something by joining parts
verbs.wrong: To store something in its place
verbs.why: We put together a simple dinner from leftovers. He put together a great outfit for the wedding. This year, many shoppers put together their own costumes from thrift-store clothing.

verbs.correct: To manage with what you have
verbs.wrong: To fix something that is broken
verbs.why: We had no butter, so we made do with oil. The team made do with an old bus for the trip. Some TikTok users make do with whatever they already have at home.

chunks.text: Homemade costumes are not new on TikTok. Last October, a [[trend tracker]] from Vogue Business counted more than 22,000 posts under a tag for homemade costumes. According to the tracker, creators take [[thrifted finds]] and household materials and {{turn them into}} [[polished]] looks. They {{show off}} the whole process in [[sped-up]] videos. The trend is strongest around Halloween. It also continues all year, through fan conventions and festival fashion.

verbs.correct: To make something become something new
verbs.wrong: To return something to a store
verbs.why: She turned an old shirt into a bag. They turned the garage into a small office. Creators take thrifted finds and household materials and turn them into polished costumes.

verbs.correct: To show something proudly to others
verbs.wrong: To sell something at a low price
verbs.why: He loves to show off his new car. The kids showed off their drawings to their grandparents. Costume creators show off the whole process in sped-up videos.

chunks.text: A survey released in late September shows the same [[shift]] among shoppers. It was [[commissioned]] by Goodwill, the thrift-store [[charity]], and asked 2,000 American adults who buy or make costumes. It found that 85 percent plan to use thrift shopping or homemade pieces this year. More than half {{turn to}} thrift stores to [[save money]]. And 44 percent go there to {{pick up}} [[materials]] for a homemade look. Seventy-one percent want pieces they can {{hold on to}} and use again after Halloween.

verbs.correct: To go to someone or somewhere for help
verbs.wrong: To work at a place without pay
verbs.why: When I need advice, I turn to my older sister. Many families turn to food banks at the end of the month. In the survey, more than half of the shoppers turn to thrift stores to save money.

verbs.wrong: To fix a hole in clothing
verbs.why: I picked up a nice lamp at a yard sale. She picked up two shirts for five dollars. In the survey, 44 percent go to thrift stores to pick up materials for a homemade look.

verbs.correct: To keep something for later use
verbs.wrong: To wash something before wearing it
verbs.why: I always hold on to my receipts for a month. You should hold on to that coat for next winter. Seventy-one percent of the shoppers want costume pieces they can hold on to and use again.

chunks.text: [[Store-bought]] costumes are still [[big business]]. The National Retail Federation expects Americans to {{shell out}} $13.5 billion on Halloween this year, up from $13.1 billion in 2025. That includes $4.4 billion on costumes. Fewer people now {{look up}} costume ideas online, 32 percent compared with 37 percent last year. Most still {{go for}} [[classic]] characters. About 4.8 million plan to be a witch and 4.2 million a vampire. A federation official said shoppers are paying close attention to prices this season.

verbs.correct: To spend a lot of money
verbs.wrong: To borrow money from a bank
verbs.why: We shelled out a lot for concert tickets. Parents shell out hundreds of dollars for school supplies. Americans are expected to shell out $13.5 billion on Halloween this year.

verbs.correct: To find facts or ideas online
verbs.why: I looked up the bus times on my phone. She looks up new recipes every weekend. In the federation's survey, 32 percent look up costume ideas online, down from 37 percent.

verbs.wrong: To wait in line for something
verbs.why: I think I'll go for the chicken salad. Most buyers go for the cheaper model. Most adults still go for classic characters, such as a witch or a vampire.

mainIdea.s: This year, many Americans plan to make Halloween costumes from used clothes and things they have at home. Surveys show people want to save money, but total spending is still rising.
mainIdea.why: In one survey, 85 percent of shoppers plan to use thrift shopping or homemade pieces. Spending is still expected to reach $13.5 billion.

mainIdea.s: Homemade costumes are popular this fall, and many shoppers are turning to thrift stores. Because of this change, Americans will spend less on Halloween this year than they did in 2025.
mainIdea.why: Close, but spending is going up, not down. Americans are expected to shell out $13.5 billion, compared with $13.1 billion in 2025.

mainIdea.s: Several large stores have stopped selling Halloween costumes for children after safety complaints. Parents now have fewer choices, and some shops say prices may climb before Halloween.
mainIdea.why: No stores stopped selling costumes. Many people put together their own costumes from thrift-store clothing and household objects.

lines.text: Do you have plans for Halloween?
A party, but I haven't decided what to {{dress up as}} yet.
I've been watching TikTok videos where people {{put together}} costumes from thrift-store clothes.
I've seen those! They take old stuff and {{turn it into}} something amazing.
And they {{show off}} every step in those sped-up videos. It's very [[satisfying to watch]].
Is it really cheaper than buying a costume?
Usually. A survey for Goodwill found that more than half of shoppers {{turn to}} thrift stores to save money.
Makes me think of my closet. I could probably {{make do with}} what I already own.
I like that. Halloween [[on a shoestring]].
I might still {{pick up}} a few things, like a hat or a cape.
Sure. Most people want pieces they can {{hold on to}} and wear again, too.
Smart. Store costumes can feel like [[money down the drain]].
People still {{shell out}} a lot, though. Halloween spending is expected to hit $13.5 billion.
Wow. So what costumes are most adults choosing?
Most {{go for}} classic characters. Witches and vampires are at the top.
Then I'll {{look up}} some ideas tonight and try to [[think outside the box]].
Good plan. Just don't leave it [[until the last minute]].

expressions.def: Used about money that is wasted
ex: That gym membership was money down the drain.

expressions.def: To think in a new and creative way, not the usual way
ex: The team had no money for ads, so they had to think outside the box.

expressions.def: Used to say someone waits too long to do something
ex: He never packs until the last minute.
